title: Glipizide and Alcohol: Low Blood Sugar Risks and Safe Drinking
excerpt: Can you drink on glipizide? Why glipizide and alcohol can cause delayed low blood sugar, who's most at risk, how to drink more safely, and when to call 911.
metaDescription: Can you drink on glipizide? Why glipizide and alcohol can cause delayed low blood sugar, how to drink more safely, and the warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** glipizide and alcohol can be a risky mix because both lower your blood sugar, and alcohol can keep pulling it down for many hours after your last drink. Glipizide (brand names Glucotrol and Glucotrol XL) works by squeezing extra insulin out of your pancreas. Alcohol stops your liver from releasing the backup sugar your body normally uses to correct a dip. Put the two together and you can end up with low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), often hours later, frequently overnight while you're asleep. Many people on glipizide can still have an occasional drink, but only with their doctor's agreement and a few non-negotiable precautions.

**The quick rules:** Never drink on an empty stomach. Ask your prescriber whether any alcohol is okay for you on glipizide, and if so, how much; that limit should come from them, not from a general guideline. Check your blood sugar before you drink, before bed, and when you wake up. Eat a snack before sleeping if your doctor recommends it. Carry fast sugar, and wear a medical ID. Don't skip or double your glipizide dose to "make room" for drinks without talking to your doctor first.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how glipizide and alcohol interact in general terms. It is not a substitute for advice from a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, your dose, and your other medicines. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on glipizide**, especially if you've had low blood sugar before, have kidney or liver problems, are over 65, take insulin or beta-blockers, or drink more than a little. **Call 911 if** someone on glipizide is confused, can't swallow safely, has a seizure, or can't be woken up. Treat it as low blood sugar first; don't assume they're just drunk.

## How Glipizide Works (and Why That Matters for Drinking)

Glipizide belongs to a group of diabetes medicines called **sulfonylureas**. Others in the group include glimepiride (Amaryl) and glyburide. They all work the same basic way: they tell the insulin-making cells in your pancreas to release more insulin.

That's a useful way to bring down high blood sugar, but it has one important quirk. **Sulfonylureas push insulin out whether or not your blood sugar actually needs it.** If you've eaten a normal meal, the extra insulin moves sugar from your blood into your cells and things balance out. If you haven't eaten, or something else is already lowering your blood sugar, the extra insulin can push you too low.

This is why sulfonylureas are known for causing low blood sugar more often than some other diabetes medicines. Metformin, for comparison, works mainly by reducing how much sugar your liver makes and rarely causes lows on its own. (If you take metformin too, see our separate guide on [metformin and alcohol](/never-hungover/metformin-and-alcohol), which covers a different risk.)

There are two forms of glipizide:

- **Regular (immediate-release) glipizide** is usually taken about 30 minutes before a meal, once or twice a day. Its effect builds over the first few hours.
- **Glipizide XL (extended-release)** is taken once a day and releases the drug slowly, so its effect lasts around the clock.

Either way, the drug's effect can last well beyond the time you took the pill. That's important, because alcohol's effect on blood sugar also stretches out over many hours.

## The Interaction: Why Glipizide and Alcohol Can Drop Your Blood Sugar

Your body has a backup system for keeping blood sugar steady between meals and overnight. When your blood sugar starts to fall, your liver releases sugar, either from its stored supply (glycogen) or by making new sugar from scratch, a process called **gluconeogenesis**. This is what keeps you from going low while you sleep.

Alcohol interferes with that backup system in a few ways:

1. **Your liver puts alcohol first.** The liver treats alcohol as a toxin to clear, and while it's busy breaking alcohol down, it largely stops making new sugar. The chemical changes that happen inside liver cells while processing alcohol directly block gluconeogenesis.
2. **Stored sugar runs low.** If you've drunk on an empty stomach, or you're drinking late at night after dinner has worn off, your liver's glycogen stores may already be low. Without new sugar being made, there's little left to fall back on.
3. **Your body's warning signals get dulled.** Alcohol can blunt the hormone response and the physical warning signs that normally alert you to a low.

Now add glipizide. It's still telling your pancreas to release insulin, which keeps moving sugar out of your blood. Normally your liver would release sugar to make up the difference. With alcohol on board, it can't keep up. The result is a blood sugar level that keeps sliding down.

### Why the low is often delayed

This is the part that catches people out. Blood sugar may look fine, or even high, while you're actually drinking, especially if you're having beer, cider, sweet cocktails, or sugary mixers. The drop often comes later, as the carbohydrates wear off and your liver is still occupied with alcohol.

Diabetes organizations, including the American Diabetes Association, warn that alcohol can lower blood sugar for **up to 24 hours** after drinking. In practice the riskiest window is often overnight and the next morning: you've gone to bed, you're not eating, glipizide is still active (especially the XL form), and your liver's backup system is offline.

### The "I just feel drunk" problem

Low blood sugar and being drunk look remarkably alike. Both can cause:

- Confusion or trouble thinking clearly
- Slurred speech
- Dizziness and poor balance
- Blurred vision
- Drowsiness
- Mood changes or irritability

That overlap is dangerous in two directions. You may not realize you're going low because you assume you're tipsy. And the people around you may assume you've had too much to drink and let you "sleep it off," when what you actually need is sugar. This is why a medical ID and telling a friend you have diabetes really matter.

## Does Glipizide Cause a Flushing Reaction With Alcohol?

You may have seen warnings that sulfonylureas can cause a reaction with alcohol similar to the drug disulfiram (Antabuse): a red, hot face, pounding headache, nausea, and a racing heart. This reaction is classically linked to an older first-generation sulfonylurea called **chlorpropamide**, which is rarely used today.

With glipizide and the other newer sulfonylureas, this kind of reaction has been reported only rarely. Low blood sugar is a far more common and more serious concern. Still, if you notice unusual flushing, a throbbing headache, or nausea soon after drinking on glipizide, stop drinking and mention it to your doctor. (If you flush with alcohol even without medication, our guide on [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers other common causes.)

## Who Is Most at Risk of Lows on Glipizide

Some people are more likely to have serious low blood sugar when they combine glipizide and alcohol. You're at higher risk if you:

- **Are older.** People over 65 are generally more sensitive to sulfonylureas and more likely to have severe lows.
- **Have kidney or liver problems.** Your liver is your blood sugar backup, and it also clears glipizide. Kidney problems can change how your body handles the drug too.
- **Skip meals or eat irregularly.** Glipizide without food is already a recipe for lows. Alcohol makes it worse.
- **Take more than one diabetes medicine**, especially insulin. The effects add up.
- **Take a beta-blocker** (such as metoprolol or propranolol). These blood pressure and heart medicines can hide the shaky, racing-heart warning signs of a low.
- **Exercise the same day.** Dancing at a party or an afternoon hike plus evening drinks can drain your sugar stores further.
- **Have had a severe low before**, or have trouble noticing your lows (sometimes called hypoglycemia unawareness).
- **Drink heavily or binge.** The more alcohol, the longer your liver's backup system stays offline.

If any of these describe you, the conversation with your doctor about drinking is especially worth having.

## How to Drink More Safely on Glipizide

If your doctor says an occasional drink is okay for you, these are the habits that make the biggest difference. None of them make alcohol risk-free on glipizide, but they lower the chance of a dangerous low.

### Before you drink

- **Ask your doctor first.** Ask specifically: how many drinks are reasonable for me, should I change anything about my glipizide on days I drink, and what blood sugar number should I aim for at bedtime?
- **Check your blood sugar.** If it's already low or on the low side, eat first and hold off on drinking.
- **Eat a real meal.** Food with carbohydrate and protein gives your body something to work with. Drinking on an empty stomach is the single riskiest thing you can do on glipizide.
- **Don't change your dose on your own.** Skipping glipizide can send your blood sugar high; taking it and then not eating can send it low. Get a plan from your doctor or pharmacist instead of guessing.

### While you drink

- **Stick to your prescriber's limit.** General diabetes guidance exists, but glipizide adds its own low-blood-sugar risk, so the amount that's okay for you (if any) should come from the doctor who knows your dose, kidneys, and history.
- **Go slowly.** Sip, and alternate each alcoholic drink with water or a sugar-free drink.
- **Snack as you go.** Keep some carbohydrate around, especially if the night runs long.
- **Watch the mixers.** Sugary mixers, sweet wines, and many cocktails can spike your blood sugar early on, which can make you think you're fine, then the drop comes later. Diet mixers avoid the spike, but they don't protect you from the later low.
- **Tell someone.** Let at least one person you're with know you have diabetes, what a low looks like, and what to do.
- **Carry fast sugar.** Glucose tablets or gel fit in a pocket.

### Before bed and the next morning

This is where most serious alcohol-related lows happen, so it deserves the most attention.

- **Check your blood sugar before you sleep.** Many doctors suggest eating a snack with carbohydrate before bed after drinking, and some set a higher bedtime target on drinking nights. Ask yours what number to aim for.
- **Don't go to bed low.** If you're below your target, treat it and recheck before sleeping.
- **Set an alarm or ask someone to check on you** if you've had more than usual. A continuous glucose monitor (CGM) with low alerts is especially useful on these nights if you have one.
- **Check again when you wake up**, and eat breakfast. Don't skip breakfast because you feel rough; that's when you need fuel most.
- **Stay alert for the next 24 hours.** A low can still come the following afternoon, especially if you're also not eating much.

## Recognizing and Treating a Low

Know these signs well, and make sure the people you drink with know them too.

**Early signs of low blood sugar:**

- Shakiness or trembling
- Sweating, chills, or clamminess
- Fast heartbeat
- Hunger
- Anxiety, nervousness, or irritability
- Lightheadedness or dizziness
- Tingling around the lips

**Signs it's getting worse:**

- Confusion or trouble concentrating
- Slurred speech or clumsiness
- Blurred vision
- Extreme sleepiness or weakness
- Seizures or loss of consciousness

Shakiness is worth special mention. Plenty of people get the shakes the morning after drinking without having diabetes (we cover the usual reasons in our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes)). On glipizide, though, morning shakiness should always prompt a blood sugar check before you assume it's "just a hangover."

### The 15-15 rule

If you're awake and able to swallow, the standard approach most diabetes educators teach is:

1. **Take about 15 grams of fast-acting sugar.** That's about 4 ounces (half a cup) of juice or regular soda, 3 to 4 glucose tablets, or a tablespoon of sugar or honey.
2. **Wait 15 minutes and recheck.** If you're still below 70 mg/dL, repeat.
3. **Eat a snack or meal once you're back up**, ideally with some protein and carbohydrate, to keep from dropping again.

Two things are different on glipizide and alcohol:

- **Lows can come back.** Glipizide keeps stimulating insulin for hours, and alcohol keeps your liver offline. A low that you treat once can return. Keep checking, and don't go back to sleep right after treating one without eating something more substantial.
- **Don't use alcohol to treat a low.** It sounds obvious, but a sweet cocktail is not a treatment. The sugar may help briefly, but the alcohol makes the bigger problem worse.

### When to call 911

Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone on glipizide:

- Is confused and can't safely eat or drink
- Has a seizure
- Passes out or can't be woken up
- Doesn't improve after treating a low, or keeps going low

Don't try to pour liquid into the mouth of someone who isn't fully awake, because they can choke. If they have a glucagon kit and someone has been shown how to use it, use it and still call 911. Glucagon works by making the liver release stored sugar, and it may work less well when those stores are depleted by alcohol or fasting, which is one more reason to get emergency help rather than wait.

Severe lows caused by sulfonylureas often need hospital monitoring, because the drug can keep blood sugar low for a long time even after initial treatment.

## Glipizide, Alcohol, and High Blood Sugar

Lows get most of the attention, but alcohol can push blood sugar the other way too. Beer, cider, sweet wine, liqueurs, and cocktails with juice or regular soda contain a lot of carbohydrate. In the first few hours, these can raise your blood sugar. Then, as the carbohydrates are used up and alcohol keeps the liver busy, you can swing low.

This rollercoaster is why it's tempting to make a mistake: seeing a high number while drinking and taking extra medication, or skipping the bedtime snack. Don't take extra glipizide to correct a high reading while you're drinking unless your doctor has specifically told you to. For a broader picture of how different drinks affect blood sugar, see our [alcohol and diabetes blood sugar management guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

Regular heavy drinking also tends to make diabetes harder to manage over time. It adds calories, can raise triglycerides and blood pressure, and is linked to nerve damage and liver disease, which are already concerns for people with diabetes. If you find you're drinking more than you'd like, it's worth raising with your doctor, who can help without judgment.

## Glipizide vs Other Diabetes Medicines With Alcohol

Different diabetes medicines carry different alcohol risks. Here's a rough comparison to help you understand where glipizide sits. Your own risk depends on your dose, your other medicines, and your health, so check with your doctor.

| Medicine type | Examples | Main alcohol concern |
|---|---|---|
| Sulfonylureas | Glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide | Low blood sugar, often delayed and overnight |
| Insulin | Many types | Low blood sugar, often delayed and overnight |
| Metformin | Glucophage | Rare but serious lactic acidosis with heavy drinking; stomach upset |
| SGLT2 inhibitors | Jardiance, Farxiga | Dehydration and a rare acid build-up called ketoacidosis |
| GLP-1 medicines | Ozempic, Mounjaro | Nausea; possible lows when combined with sulfonylureas or insulin |

If you take glipizide together with another diabetes medicine, the risks can stack. For example, glipizide plus an SGLT2 inhibitor brings both the low blood sugar risk and the dehydration risk; see our guide to [Jardiance and alcohol](/never-hungover/jardiance-and-alcohol) for that side.

## Other Medicines That Can Make It Worse

Your pharmacist is the best person to look over your full list, but a few common combinations are worth knowing about when alcohol is in the picture:

- **Beta-blockers** can hide the warning signs of a low, as mentioned above.
- **Aspirin and other salicylates** at higher doses can add to glipizide's blood-sugar-lowering effect. A single standard dose is usually not the concern; regular high doses can be.
- **Some antibiotics and antifungals**, such as fluconazole and certain sulfa antibiotics, can increase glipizide's effect.
- **Sleep aids and other sedatives** combined with alcohol make you sleep more deeply, which makes it harder to wake up and notice a low overnight.

If you've started any new medicine recently, ask your pharmacist whether it changes how you should approach drinking on glipizide. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) also covers how supplements fit in alongside prescriptions.

## What About Hangover Supplements?

If you're on glipizide and looking into hangover supplements, be cautious. Some "hangover" and "detox" products contain extra sugar, herbal ingredients that may affect blood sugar, or ingredients that haven't been studied alongside diabetes medicines.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. Some animal research has looked at DHM and blood sugar regulation, which is exactly why you should check with your doctor before taking it alongside a medicine like glipizide. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents alcohol-related low blood sugar, and it does nothing to change how glipizide and alcohol interact.

If your doctor is comfortable with you trying it, well-reviewed options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers typical amounts and timing, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. But on glipizide, the habits above (food, moderation, bedtime checks) matter far more than any supplement. For the general habits that make hangovers less likely in the first place, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Glipizide makes your pancreas release insulin even when you don't need it, and alcohol stops your liver from releasing backup sugar. Together they can cause low blood sugar.
- The low is often **delayed**, sometimes by many hours, and is most dangerous **overnight and the next morning**.
- Low blood sugar looks a lot like being drunk, so check your blood sugar rather than guessing, and make sure someone with you knows you have diabetes.
- If your doctor says drinking is okay for you: always drink with food, stay within the limit they gave you, check before bed and on waking, carry fast sugar, and wear a medical ID.
- Don't skip, double, or shift your glipizide dose to accommodate drinking without your doctor's plan.
- Call 911 for confusion that prevents safe eating, seizures, or someone who can't be woken.

For the wider picture of why drinking can drop blood sugar even without medication, see our guide to [low blood sugar after drinking](/never-hungover/low-blood-sugar-after-drinking), and if you also take metformin, our [metformin and alcohol](/never-hungover/metformin-and-alcohol) guide covers that drug's separate risks.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I drink alcohol while taking glipizide?**

Many people with type 2 diabetes who take glipizide can have a small amount of alcohol, but only with their doctor's okay and with precautions. Glipizide makes your pancreas release insulin, and alcohol stops your liver from releasing stored sugar, so together they can cause low blood sugar. If your doctor says it's fine, stay within the limit they set, always drink with food, never drink on an empty stomach, check your blood sugar before bed, and know the signs of a low.

**How long after drinking can low blood sugar happen on glipizide?**

Low blood sugar can show up during drinking, but it's often delayed. Diabetes organizations warn that alcohol can lower blood sugar for up to 24 hours after you drink, and the most dangerous time is often overnight while you're asleep. Check your blood sugar before bed and again when you wake up, and eat a snack with carbohydrate before sleeping if your doctor recommends it.

**Should I skip my glipizide dose if I'm going to drink?**

Don't change your dose on your own. Skipping a dose can cause high blood sugar, and taking it without eating can cause lows. The right approach depends on your dose, whether you take regular or extended-release glipizide, and your blood sugar patterns. Ask your doctor or pharmacist ahead of time what to do on days you plan to drink.

**What are the signs of low blood sugar after drinking?**

Early signs include shakiness, sweating, a fast heartbeat, hunger, anxiety, irritability, and feeling lightheaded. As it gets worse you may see confusion, slurred speech, blurred vision, clumsiness, and extreme sleepiness, which look a lot like being drunk. Severe lows can cause seizures or loss of consciousness. The only way to tell a low from being tipsy is to check your blood sugar.

**How do I treat a low after drinking on glipizide?**

If you're awake and can swallow, take about 15 grams of fast sugar, like 4 ounces of juice or regular soda or glucose tablets, then recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if you're still below 70 mg/dL. Follow it with a snack that has protein and carbs. Because glipizide keeps working for hours, lows can come back, so keep checking. If someone is confused, can't swallow safely, or passes out, call 911.

**Does glipizide cause a flushing reaction with alcohol?**

A flushing reaction (red face, headache, nausea) is classically linked to an older sulfonylurea called chlorpropamide. It has been reported only rarely with newer ones like glipizide. If you notice flushing, pounding headache, or nausea after a drink on glipizide, stop drinking and tell your doctor. Low blood sugar is the far more common and more serious risk.

**Is glipizide XL safer with alcohol than regular glipizide?**

Not necessarily. Glipizide XL releases the drug slowly over the day, so its effect lasts around the clock, including overnight when alcohol-related lows tend to hit. Regular glipizide peaks within a few hours of a dose. Both forms can cause low blood sugar with alcohol. Ask your doctor how your specific form and dose fit with drinking.

**Can DHM help prevent low blood sugar from alcohol on glipizide?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents alcohol-related low blood sugar, and it does not change how glipizide and alcohol interact. DHM is a plant compound studied mostly in animals for its effects on alcohol metabolism. If you take glipizide or any diabetes medicine, ask your doctor before adding any supplement.
